name: Swinging London
hook: Mod fashion, pirate radio, and guitar bands on cheap gear, all competing to sound like the future.

blurb.age7: In London in the 1960s, young people with sharp new clothes and radios playing from ships offshore turned guitar music into something loud and exciting.
blurb.age13: By the early 1960s a generation of young working Britons had more spare money than their parents had, and mod subculture, sharp Italian-influenced fashion, scooters, imported American soul records, grew up around that. Radio stations broadcasting illegally from ships offshore, because the BBC gave recorded pop music very little air time, got the music to a mass audience the official broadcaster mostly ignored.
blurb.adult: Swinging London's mod scene is a useful case of subculture as class assertion: young people with new disposable income using style, music, and imported soul records to construct an identity distinct from both their parents' generation and traditional British class markers. Pirate stations like Radio Caroline existed specifically because BBC 'needle time' rules sharply limited recorded pop music broadcast hours, leaving a gap an offshore, unlicensed industry filled.

geopolitics: Postwar British austerity gave way to a consumer boom by the early 1960s, and young working Britons had disposable income their parents' generation mostly had not. BBC needle-time restrictions, agreed with musicians' unions to protect live broadcasting work, sharply limited recorded pop music airtime, which is what made unlicensed offshore pirate radio stations commercially viable.
whatWasNew: Guitar distortion embraced as a deliberate choice rather than a fault, mod subculture's stylistic intensity treated as inseparable from the music, and the single, not the album, as the era's primary currency.
production: Small London studios working fast on tight teenage-pop budgets and schedules, frequently with an outside producer holding more creative control than the band.
labels: A cluster of UK labels, Pye and Decca-distributed imprints like Brunswick among them, signed the era's guitar bands, generally on terms that favored the label over the artist.
politics: Less overtly political than punk or post-punk, but mod subculture functioned partly as a class-conscious style statement by young people newly able to spend on how they looked and what they listened to.
